newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gore arrives in South Africa after stop in Namibia.
newsitem.headline: Gore arrives in South Africa after stop in Namibia.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in South Africa on Friday after making a brief stop in Namibia where he urged that country's leaders not to give in to the temptation to stifle political dissent.
Gore arrived at the head of a high-level U.S. delegation for three days of talks, hoping to smooth relations recently disturbed by a proposed South African arms deal with Syria.

In talks with Namibian leaders at the airport in Windhoek, Gore praised the country's seven years of independence, saying it had been an inspiration to the world for its democracy, tolerance and environmental protection.

"It is unusual to have one political party as completely dominant in the political dialogue as you have here. That poses special challenges to nurture the opportunity for other voices to be heard," Gore said.
"I sense a determination to resist occasional voices that are heard in every country to stifle dissent," he said.

Gore plans to tour conservation projects in Durban on Saturday as well as meet with labour union leaders. He said the KwaZulu Natal region of South Africa had a bright economic future if it could remain at peace.

The Vice President then travels to Cape Town where he will head the U.S. side to the U.S.-South Africa binational commission which meets about every six months. The South African side is headed by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.

While the commission will concentrate on trade, the environment, energy, agriculture, education and science, Gore and Mbeki are likely to focus on foreign affairs in private one-on-one discussions in Cape Town.

The two countries exchanged angry words last month when the United States warned South Africa against going through with a proposed $650 million sale of a laser-guided tank firing control system to Syria, which Washington classifies as a "state sponsor of terrorism".

South African President Nelson Mandela angrily rejected the U.S. criticism as an affront to his country's national pride and independence. Washington warned providing the system to Syria would result in South Africa losing $120 million of U.S. aid.

The United States was previously upset when Mandela hosted Iranian President Akbar Rafsanjani last year. But tempers have cooled in recent weeks and the Syrian arms deal appears to be on the back burner.

Gore, who seems certain to run for president in the year 2000, has emerged as a key player in U.S. foreign policy. Last week he chaired important bilateral talks with Russia and next month will head a delegation to China.
The U.S. delegation to South Africa includes new Commerce Secretary William Daley, Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt and Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman.
Since the lifting of U.S. economic sanctions in 1993, U.S.-South African trade has increased by around half a billion dollars.
The centrepiece of the South Africa trip could be a bilateral tax treaty that will allow U.S. prospective investors to make more predictable assumptions about the taxes they are likely to face.
Gore will also pay courtesy calls on Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, tour the island prison where Mandela was held for 27 years and meet labour leaders in Durban.
